newsitem.title: CHINA: China papers publish warning on stock trade.
newsitem.headline: China papers publish warning on stock trade.

text.p: China's major newspapers published an editorial on Friday justifying the sacking of top officials of several banks and brokerages and warning that tough punishments were needed to halt stock market irregularities.
Major newspapers published an editorial of the official People's Daily saying that further supervision was needed to ensure a fair and open securities market.

"Recently, a small number of institutions and individuals have ignored the law and committed crimes despite state orders.., " said the editorial published in the China Securities newspaper as well as other key financial papers.

"They have used hundreds of millions of yuan as improper funds to stir up trading on the securities market, damaging the interests of investors and interfering with normal market order," the editorial said.
The newspaper warned that authorities would act according to the law and pursue violators, adding that laws would be strictly implemented.

China said on Thursday it had sacked the head of the Shanghai branch of the big state-run Industrial and Commercial Bank Shen Ruolei for allowing bank funds to be used to finance trading in the stock market.

The official media also said authorities had sacked the head of the Shenzhen Development Bank, one of the blue chip companies on the Shenzhen stock exchange, for dealing in the bank's own shares and had seized 90 million yuan ($10.8 million) in profits from those trades.

At the same time, authorities replaced the heads of three big brokerage houses, Shenyin & Wanguo, Haitong and Guangdong Development (Guangfa) Securities for using bank funds to speculate in the stock market. The three brokerages were also fined and banned from trading on their own account for one year.
Chinese authorities have been trying to shut off a flow of funds from the banking sector into the stock market to limit risk to the financial system.
They have issued a series of warnings and new regulations to keep bank funds out of what they see as excessively speculative investments.

State media also confirmed an earlier report that authorities had dismissed both the chairman and chief accountant of Guangshen Railway Co Ltd, a Chinese company listed in Hong Kong and with American depositary receipts trading in New York.

Newspapers said Guangshen, which operates the rail link between Shenzhen and the Guangdong provincial capital of Guangzhou, had placed 300 million yuan raised from its initial public offer with J&A International Finance, which had in turn extended the funds to J&A Securities for investment in the stock market.
China ordered the funds returned and barred J&A Securities, a major brokerage based in Shenzhen, from trading on its own account for six months. ($1 = 8.3 yuan)
